name: Mjölnir
powers: Summons thunder and lightning; returns to the thrower's hand; hallows weddings and funerals.
description: The mighty hammer of Thor, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri as the prize of a wager Loki made on his own head. The hammer's handle came out short because Loki, in fly form, bit the dwarf's hand while he worked the bellows. Mjölnir could shatter mountains, was thrown like a boomerang, and also served to consecrate marriages, births, and funerals. Thor's iron gloves Járngreipr are needed to grip its scorching shaft.

name: Megingjörð
powers: Doubles the god's already godlike strength.
description: The belt of the thunder god Thor which, when he girds it on, doubles his strength. It is named in the Prose Edda alongside his iron gloves Járngreipr as one of the three great possessions of Thor, the third being the hammer Mjölnir. Without it Thor is still mighty; with it, nothing among the giants can stand against him.

name: The Mistletoe Spear
powers: The only thing that could kill Baldr, who had sworn protection against all other things.
description: The mistletoe shaft with which the blind god Höðr, guided by Loki, slew Baldr the beloved. Only the mistletoe had not sworn to spare him, and Loki fetched it, fashioned it into a dart, and guided Höðr's hand. The killing of Baldr by the mistletoe spear set the doom of the gods in motion and stands at the centre of the Eddic tragedy.

name: The Magic Churn
powers: Dairy magic that brings or steals the butter.
description: A butter churn that witches were believed to bewitch or to work from afar. In Swedish folk belief a witch (trollkona) could send a 'mjölkhare', a butter or cream hare, to steal milk from neighbours' cows and churns, or charm a churn so that butter would not come. Counter-magic included heating a knife in the fire and running it through the churn to break the spell.
source: Swedish folk belief about milk and butter magic

name: The Magic Scythe
maker: Given as a wonder-gift in the tale
powers: Mows grain by itself, without a hand to swing it.
description: A scythe in Swedish folktales that cuts grain by itself, without a hand to swing it. In the tale of the magic scythe, the wonderful tool performs the harvest work of many men, sparing its owner the labour of mowing. The self-working scythe belongs to a family of Swedish wonder-tools in which ordinary farm implements act on their own.

name: The Magic Table
aliases: Table, the Ass and the Stick
maker: Given as a wonder-gift in the tales
powers: Sets itself with food and drink at a word.
description: A table that sets itself with food, a recurring wonder-object of Swedish folk tales. At a word the self-serving table covers itself with dishes and ale, so the hero never goes hungry; the motif usually appears in tales where a magic object is given as a reward and later stolen and replaced with a worthless copy. It belongs to the family of self-working marvels in Swedish wonder-tales.
source: Swedish wonder-tale motif of the self-setting table

name: The Magician's Cape
maker: Worn by the magician of the tale
powers: Lets the wearer fly, turn invisible, or work spells.
description: A cape that gives its wearer magical power in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Magician's Cape', the cloak lets the hero fly, become invisible, or work spells, and is won, lost, and recovered through the story's tests. The cape is a classic object of wonder-tales: a garment of ordinary cut that carries extraordinary ability.

name: Midsummer Maypole
maker: Raised by the village at Midsummer
powers: Centre of the Midsummer dance and fertility rites.
description: The midsummer pole (midsommarstång or majstång), a tall pole decorated with greenery, flowers, and rings, raised on Midsummer Eve and danced around in Swedish tradition. Songs, ring-dances, and games circle the pole, and the custom is recorded in Sweden from the 17th century. The pole is central to the Midsummer celebration and its bonfire-night rites.

name: The Madonna's Golden Shoe
maker: Belonging to the church Madonna statue
description: The golden shoe of the Virgin Mary's statue, at the centre of the Swedish tale 'The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe'. In the tale a fiddler who plays for the church is rewarded when the Madonna herself bestows her golden shoe on him. The tale is one of Sweden's many stories of a church statue that comes alive.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe'

name: The Magic Book
powers: Grants knowledge, secrets, or magical skill to whoever reads it.
description: A book endowed with supernatural power in the Danish tale of the same name, granting its owner knowledge, hidden secrets, or magical skill, and bringing both power and danger. Magic books of this kind echo the real black books of Scandinavian folk magic, which were used to heal and to find lost things. The story belongs to the Nordic cycle of grimoire legends.
source: Danish folk tale, collected in tale collections

name: Robe of Medea
material: Robed cloth and a golden diadem, steeped in poison
powers: Bursts into flame on the wearer; destroys Glauce and her father Creon.
description: The poisoned robe and golden diadem Medea sent to Glauce, Jason's new bride at Corinth; when the princess donned them, fire consumed her and her father Creon. Euripides' Medea makes the bridal gifts the engine of her revenge, and the robe recurs as a deadly bridal-gift motif in later myth.

name: Mehter Davul
material: Wooden shell with skin heads, struck with a beater
powers: Beats the rhythm of the janissary march, inspiring troops and intimidating the enemy.
description: The great bass drum of the mehter, the Ottoman military band, slung and struck to beat the rhythm of the janissary march; its booming sound, with the zurna, was meant to inspire troops and terrify the enemy in battle, and the mehter davul remains an emblem of Ottoman martial music.
source: Ottoman musical tradition; documentation of the mehter band

name: Mantle of Tegau Eurfron
powers: Fitted only a wife faithful to her husband; exposed unfaithful wives.
description: Tegau Eurfron's mantle, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. It would fall only to a wife faithful to her husband; for a woman who had broken her vows it would not cover her, and the truth of her conduct was laid bare. It is the Welsh counterpart of the chastity-testing garments of continental romance.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: The Mace of Faridun
maker: Forged for the young prince Faridun
powers: Struck down the tyrant Zahhak and freed Iran from his reign.
description: The bull-headed mace (gurz) forged for the young prince Faridun, which Ferdowsi describes being made to his measure before his campaign against the tyrant Zahhak. With it Faridun struck Zahhak's crowned head and split the serpents on his shoulders, ending a thousand years of tyranny and binding the usurper in a mountain cave. It became the archetypal weapon of Persian hero-kings.

name: Morin Khuur
powers: Voice of the horse and the steppe
description: The two-stringed horse-head fiddle of Mongolia, its scroll carved as a horse's head and its strings and bow made of horsehair. Legend tells of a herdsman whose beloved horse was killed, and who made the fiddle from its remains to keep the horse's song alive; it is now an emblem of Mongolian national identity.

name: Macuahuitl
material: Wooden club edged with obsidian blades
powers: Slices through flesh in a single stroke; a mark of warrior rank.
description: A flat wooden sword edged with rows of razor-sharp obsidian blades, the signature weapon of Aztec warriors at the Spanish conquest. Chroniclers including Bernal Díaz describe its edge as sharp enough to behead a horse in one cut; codices and tribute lists record it as both a tool of war and a mark of rank. Captured enemies often carried the most ornate examples.
source: Conquistador chronicles (e.g. Bernal Díaz del Castillo)

name: Metate
era: From the preclassic era to the present
powers: Transforms maize into masa for the sacred staple tortilla.
description: A slightly concave stone slab used with a hand stone to grind soaked maize into masa, the heart of Mesoamerican cooking from the Olmec era to modern households. The grinding of maize is woven into myth and household ritual, appearing in codices and the Popol Vuh's account of people made from maize dough. Basalt metates with carved supports survive in huge numbers from ancient sites.

name: Medicine Bag
era: Indigenous North America to the present
powers: Holds the personal medicines given to its owner in a dream.
description: A small hide pouch carried or kept privately, holding the personal medicines, feathers, stones and charms revealed to its owner in vision or dream across many North American nations. The contents are personal and often secret, and the bag's power depends on how faithfully its owner follows the vision. Ethnographic accounts note it is never opened lightly and is buried with its owner.
source: Plains and Woodlands oral tradition and ethnography

name: Medicine Wheel
material: Arranged stones in a circle with spokes
era: From at least the late prehistoric era
powers: Mirrors the four directions and the circle of life.
description: Circles of stones laid out with radiating spokes on the high plains, the most famous in the Bighorn Mountains of Wyoming, whose alignment some studies tie to the solstices. The wheel is read as a sacred model of the cosmos, the four directions, the seasons and the human journey, a teaching that continues among Plains nations. The purpose of the oldest sites remains a matter of debate.
source: Plains oral tradition and archaeological study

name: Mama Cocha Effigy
powers: Gains the protection of the mother of the sea.
description: Small images and offerings made to Mama Cocha, the mother of the sea, honored by the Inca for the fish, shells and travel she provided along the Pacific coast. Fisherfolk made offerings of shell and stone at the shore, and colonial accounts record the goddess among the household and regional deities the Inca honored. The amulets carry her power out to the boats that worked her waters.
source: Colonial chronicles of Inca religion and coastal offerings

name: Mate Gourd
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Shared in a circle that marks friendship and trust.
description: The dried gourd cup in which yerba mate, the leafy infusion of the Guaraní, is drunk through a metal straw, passed hand to hand in a fixed order among friends in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. The Guaraní drank the herb before the Spanish arrived, and sharing one gourd marks closeness; etiquette governs who pours and who drinks next. It remains the everyday companion of millions.
source: Guaraní tradition and colonial accounts of mate

name: Mapinguari Claw
material: Curved claw or talisman made from it
era: Amazonian folk belief to the present
powers: Carries the strength and warning of the forest being.
description: The great claw of the Mapinguari, the shaggy, one-eyed giant of the Amazon, whose backward feet and awful stench drive hunters from his forest; the curved claw is kept as a charm or proof of a close encounter. Stories tie him to the giant ground sloths whose bones still surface in the rivers, the claw recalling both myth and memory of the deep forest. He spares the hunter who shows respect.

name: Maasai Nborr Collar
description: The nborr is a flat, beaded collar of the Maasai of Kenya, built on a leather or wire base and covered with glass-bead patterns in red, white, blue, and black. Worn by women at ceremonies and by young men (moran), the collars signal age-set, status, and clan, and beaded colours carry agreed social meanings.

name: Maasai Rungu Club
description: The rungu is a short wooden throwing club of the Maasai of Kenya, with a knobbed head and tapering handle, carried by herders and moran. Traditionally used to guard cattle against predators and in ceremony, the rungu today is a symbol of authority, often ornamented and carried by elders at gatherings.

name: Maasai Shuka Cloth
era: Contemporary, evolving from traditional hide cloth
description: The shuka is the checked, blanket-like cloth worn wrapped around the body by Maasai of Kenya and Tanzania, traditionally dyed in red tones. Red is said to honour Maasai cattle culture and the warrior ideal; the cloth's patterns vary by community, and modern production blends factory cotton with older styles of hide and woven dress.

name: Makonde Shetani Figure
description: Makonde 'shetani' carvings of Tanzania are dark hardwood figures of contorted, expressive spirits, made by Makonde carvers from the 1950s onward. They depict shetani - capricious ancestral and bush spirits - in twisted poses that blur human and animal form, and are celebrated in Swahili and international art as a meditation on the spirit world.

name: Mahafaly Aloalo Funerary Post
description: The aloalo are tall carved funerary posts of the Mahafaly people of southwestern Madagascar, erected on family tombs and topped with figures of people, birds (often the cattle egret), and cattle. Their scenes honour the life and wealth of the deceased and the ancestors, and they stand as public memorials bound to the island's ancestral rites.

name: Mbira Dzavadzimu
description: The mbira dzavadzimu is the lamellophone of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a wooden board with metal keys mounted over a gourd resonator that buzzes with a shell or bottle-top. Played to summon the ancestors (vadzimu) at ceremonies, its interlocking patterns accompany singing and call the spirits to guide the community.

name: Makonde Lipiko Mask
description: Lipiko masks of the Makonde of Mozambique are wooden face masks with protruding lips and painted detail, worn by initiates in the mapiko dance that closes initiation rites. The performers are said to embody spirits of the dead and ancestors, and the masks are kept hidden from the uninitiated.

name: Tagine Cooking Vessel
description: The tagine is the conical clay cooking vessel of Morocco, whose tall lid traps steam so that slow-braised stews cook in very little water. The same word names the dish it cooks; the pot is glazed, set over a brazier or stove, and has become emblematic of Moroccan cooking and hospitality across North Africa.

name: Mangal Kalasha
description: Copper or clay pot filled with water and topped with a coconut and mango leaves, set on a bed of rice to open Hindu ceremonies. The kalasha is treated as a vessel of the divine, inviting a presiding deity to dwell in its water, and it is carried before brides, raised at temple consecrations and used in house blessings as a source of prosperity and good fortune.
source: Hindu ritual manuals (grihya sutra tradition) and festival practice

name: Mangalsutra
description: Necklace of black beads and gold, or a gold pendant on a cord, tied by the groom around the bride's neck during the Hindu wedding rite. The mangalsutra is worn for the rest of the married woman's life and is read in folklore as a powerful talisman of her husband's life and of the marriage bond, never to be removed or broken.
source: Hindu wedding ritual and marriage custom

name: Mukut Crown
description: Jewel-set crown of the Malla and Shah kings of Nepal, worn at state and religious ceremonies and linked to the goddess Taleju, protector of the royal dynasties. The Newar tradition of the living goddess Kumari also includes a crown placed on the girl deity during festivals, echoing the belief that the right to rule comes by divine favour.
source: Newar court tradition and museum regalia holdings

name: Mani Wall
description: Long low wall of carved stones inscribed with the mantra Om Mani Padme Hum, raised beside mountain paths in the Himalayas as a prayer in stone. Travellers pass the mani wall keeping it to their right and add their own stones, so that the wall grows as a living offering along the route, and the carved stones are believed to carry blessing to all who walk by.

name: Message Stick
description: Carved wooden stick sent between Aboriginal groups to carry news and to validate the authority of the messenger. The patterns cut and painted on its surface record the message and the sender's clan identity, and the stick is accepted as proof that the bearer speaks with the consent of the people who sent them.
source: Colonial ethnographic records; Aboriginal oral tradition

name: Mere Pounamu
description: Short broad-bladed club of the Māori, carved from pounamu, the prized greenstone of Aotearoa, and regarded as a chiefly weapon and heirloom. The mere has a wide leaf-shaped blade and a rounded grip with a wrist cord, and named blades were handed down for generations, their tapu so great that they were never allowed to touch the ground.
maker: Māori carvers of the South Island pounamu sources
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori weaponry and taonga

name: Marquesan War Club (Uʻu)
description: Polished war club of the Marquesas Islands, carved from ironwood with a long shaft and a flattened head, sometimes inlaid with the teeth of the whale or the bones of enemies. The uʻu was the principal weapon of the Marquesan warrior and was also a treasured gift, its elaborate carving a record of the man who bore it and his ancestry.

name: Marshall Islands Stick Chart
description: Navigation chart of the Marshall Islands built from pandanus ribs and coconut fibre, with cowrie shells marking islands and the curved sticks recording the pattern of ocean swells. Read by trained navigators before a voyage, the charts encode the wave and current knowledge of the Pacific, and the same skill guided the first navigators across the atolls.
material: pandanus ribs, coconut fibre, cowrie shells
